options.text: The logarithm series arises because 1/n is the coefficient of the harmonic series in closed form
options.misconception: confuses the harmonic series with a logarithmic closed form

questions.explanation: Antiderivating the geometric series 1/(1 - t) term by term divides each coefficient by n+1, which yields the power series of ln(1 + x). Multiplication alone cannot create an antiderivative.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a term-by-term derivative of a binomial series at an interior point
questions.stem: The apiary notebook records the binomial expansion (1 + x)^(1/2) = 1 + x/2 - x^2/8 + x^3/16 - ... . Using the termwise derivative of this binomial series, find the value of the sum with terms n times C(1/2, n) times (0.5)^(n-1) at x = 0.5, rounding to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: Differentiating (1+x)^(1/2) term by term gives the series with terms n times C(1/2, n) x^(n-1) equal to (1/2)(1+x)^(-1/2) for |x| < 1. At x = 0.5 this is 0.5 times 1 over the square root of 1.5, that is 0.4082483.
questions.hint: Differentiate (1+x)^(1/2) and substitute x = 0.5.

options.text: The radius is 1, and at x = 0.5 the twice-differentiated series sums to 4, since 1/(1 - x)^2 equals 4 there
options.misconception: uses the first derivative formula instead of the second

options.text: The radius is infinite, and at x = 0.5 the twice-differentiated series sums to 16

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Uniform convergence on a closed subinterval
questions.learningObjective: State what uniform convergence on a closed subinterval gives and why a stronger claim fails
questions.stem: An entry in the hive notes claims that a series with radius 1 is uniformly convergent on the closed interval from -1 to 1. Write an explanation that shows what uniform convergence on a closed subinterval such as the interval from -1/2 to 1/2 gives and why the claim as stated is too strong.

answer.exemplar: A power series converges uniformly on every closed subinterval strictly inside its radius of convergence, so the series is uniformly convergent on the interval from -1/2 to 1/2 because that interval lies strictly inside the interval from -1 to 1. Uniform convergence on the closed interval from -1 to 1 cannot be claimed from the radius alone: the endpoints may even diverge, and uniform convergence on a closed interval would force the endpoint values to agree with the limit, so the series must be checked there separately.

questions.explanation: Uniform convergence is guaranteed on closed subintervals strictly inside the radius, and only there by the radius alone. Extending that claim to the endpoints requires separate analysis of the boundary points.
questions.hint: Ask how far the interval sits inside the radius.

questions.learningObjective: Justify continuity of a power series inside its radius of convergence
questions.stem: Whenever a limit is taken of a power series at a point inside its radius of convergence, is the limit of the sums equal to the value of the series at that point?

options.text: Yes, inside the radius convergence is uniform near the point, so the limit equals the series value there
No, a power series can be discontinuous at any point inside its radius
options.misconception: believes power series are discontinuous inside their radius

options.text: Yes, but only when the series is absolutely convergent at that point
options.misconception: confuses pointwise continuity with the uniform convergence that is actually used

options.text: No, because the limit of a power series at an interior point can differ from its value
options.misconception: denies continuity of a power series inside its radius

questions.explanation: Inside the radius a power series converges uniformly on compact subintervals, so it is continuous there and the limit of the sum at an interior point equals its value at that point.
questions.hint: Uniform convergence on compact subintervals forces continuity.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Determine what must hold for a grouping to preserve the value of a series
questions.stem: One apiary question asks what must be true of the series of block sums for a grouping to preserve the value of the original series. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The sign of each block decides nothing; what matters is whether the series of block sums converges
If the blocks all have the same sign the grouped series always converges
options.misconception: confuses a sign condition with convergence of the block series

options.text: Blocks must have strictly decreasing magnitudes for the grouping to preserve the value
options.misconception: attaches a decreasing-magnitude requirement that grouping does not need

options.text: Grouping an oscillating series is never valid unless the series is absolutely convergent
options.misconception: requires absolute convergence where convergence alone suffices

questions.explanation: Grouping produces a new series whose terms are the block sums, and that new series must be analysed on its own terms. If it converges, its value equals the original; if it diverges, the original may still diverge.
questions.hint: Study the series of block sums, not the original signs.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Compute the sum of a rearrangement that takes three positive terms and one negative term
questions.stem: The keeper evaluates a rearrangement of the alternating harmonic series that takes three positive terms and then one negative term, producing 1 + 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/2 + 1/7 + 1/9 + 1/11 - 1/4 + ... . Compute the sum of this rearranged series to four decimal places.
questions.explanation: After m groups the partial sum is H_{6m} - (1/2)H_{3m} - (1/2)H_m, and the harmonic asymptotic gives the limit ln 2 + (1/2) ln 3 = 1.2424534, rounding to 1.2425, which differs from ln 2.
questions.hint: The partial sum after m groups is H_{6m} - H_{3m}/2 - H_m/2.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Summing a logarithm series term by term
questions.learningObjective: Correct a confusion between the divergence of an integral and the behaviour of a series
questions.stem: A volunteer in the apiary claims the integral of the geometric series from 0 to 2 is infinite and reads that as a statement about the series of partial sums. What is wrong with the interpretation?

options.text: The integral diverges at x = 1 since the integrand blows up; that is a fact about the integral, not the series
The claim is correct, since the integral of a divergent geometric sum must also diverge everywhere
options.misconception: links divergence of the integrated series to divergence of the integrand

options.text: The logarithm never blows up, so the integral must actually be finite at x = 1
options.misconception: assumes the closed form stays finite at a pole

options.text: The integral is wrong because the antiderivative should have been ln(1 - x) with a positive sign
options.misconception: mislabels the sign of the antiderivative

questions.explanation: At x = 1 the integrand 1/(1 - t) has a non-integrable singularity, so the improper integral diverges. That is a statement about the integrand, not about the series of partial sums.
questions.hint: Separate the question about the integral from the series.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Read binomial series partial sums against the closed form
questions.stem: A final table in the apiary log lists binomial coefficients for (1 + x)^(1/2) as 1, 0.5, -0.125, 0.0625 and -0.0390625 with their contributions at x = 0.5 as 1, 0.25, -0.03125, 0.0078125 and -0.0024414. Which reading is correct?

options.text: The partial sums oscillate around 1.2247449, which equals the square root of 1.5, so the series converges to it
The partial sums settle at 1.25, the value of the first two terms added together
options.misconception: treats an early partial sum as the limit

options.text: The partial sums drift upward without bound, since the coefficients grow in magnitude
options.misconception: misreads the oscillating coefficients as unbounded growth

options.text: The partial sums settle at 1.0, the constant term of the binomial expansion
options.misconception: identifies the first term with the whole sum

questions.explanation: The tabulated partial sums oscillate with shrinking steps about 1.2247449, the value of (1 + 0.5)^(1/2) = sqrt(1.5). The binomial series converges to the closed form for |x| < 1.
questions.hint: Compare the oscillating partial sums with the square root of 1.5.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.learningObjective: Prove with nth roots that a second derivative does not shrink the radius
questions.stem: Another entry explains, using nth roots, why taking a second derivative does not shrink the radius of convergence. Write that explanation.

answer.exemplar: Differentiating twice replaces the coefficient a_n by n(n-1)a_n. The root test radius is R = 1/limsup |a_n|^(1/n), and the new coefficients have nth roots equal to |a_n|^(1/n) times (n(n-1))^(1/n). The factor (n(n-1))^(1/n) tends to 1, so the limsup is unchanged and the twice-differentiated series has exactly the same radius of convergence as the original.

questions.explanation: The extra factor n(n-1) contributes an nth root that tends to 1, so the limsup defining the radius is untouched. Any finite number of differentiations leaves the radius unchanged.
questions.hint: The factor n(n-1) has an nth root that tends to one.

questions.subject: CALCULUS_II
questions.topic: Uniform convergence on a closed subinterval
questions.learningObjective: State the standard uniform convergence guarantee for a power series
questions.stem: Which statement about uniform convergence of a power series on a closed subinterval is correct?

options.text: A power series converges uniformly on every closed subinterval strictly inside its radius of convergence
A power series converges uniformly on the closed interval spanning its radius, from -R to R
options.misconception: extends the uniform convergence guarantee to the boundary circle

options.text: A power series converges uniformly only on intervals that are symmetric about the center
options.misconception: requires symmetry of the interval, which is irrelevant to the theorem

options.text: A power series converges uniformly only where its terms all have the same sign
options.misconception: attaches a sign condition to the uniform convergence theorem

questions.explanation: The Weierstrass M-test applied on a closed subinterval strictly inside the radius gives uniform convergence there. Nothing about symmetry or sign is required, and the boundary is not covered.
questions.hint: Inside the radius the M-test applies on any closed subinterval.
